doc.title: Scott Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe,Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Variety of work in New York versus lack of a steady group
summary: He plays everything from classic jazz to Braxton and pop, but laments there is little chance to develop a sound with a regular band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Opportunities to play, do you mean in the music school situation or out of that?

Yeah. Well what I find is there’s incredible opportunities to play in an unbelievably wide variety of contexts. You know I do everything from the most classic jazz kind of thing — Marty Grosz and Peter Ecklund for example — to Anthony Braxton large orchestra, I played with the opera, I played with pop people, Elton John and people like that. In New © Hamilton Fillius Archive -4-

York particularly, it’s amazing how many different situations one finds himself in — film scores and whatnot. But what is lacking is the chance to actually have a group and play regularly, night after night with a group and develop a sound, develop a conception and a direction for your music. That’s what’s hard to do. It’s like you get plugged in here and plugged in there, and plugged in to all these different situations. But it’s really hard unless you either struggle quite a bit or unless you’re sort of one of the new young sensations or something like that then you’re able to travel with your group and play all the festivals and all of that. But that’s the element I think is missing. In the old days groups played together night after night after night after night. And that’s how the music grows.
